ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Provably-Unbiased KernelSHAP Estimation
PROPOSAL: Derive an asymptotic variance analysis for KernelSHAP, which yields an upper bound on the variance of the estimator. This result will provide insights into the trade-offs between bias and variance for KernelSHAP, a widely used but poorly understood estimator.
CONTROLS: Compare against unbiased KernelSHAP, and analyze the theoretical variance bounds for KernelSHAP on a range of synthetic datasets with known ground truth.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We expect the derived bound to provide quantitative insights into the trade-offs between bias and variance for KernelSHAP, but potentially challenge the practical performance of unbiased KernelSHAP in certain settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Non-asymptotic Bounds for KernelSHAP on Linear Models
PROPOSAL: Prove non-asymptotic bounds on the expectation and variance of KernelSHAP estimates for linear models. This will provide practical guarantees on the sample efficiency of KernelSHAP, which has been shown to be computationally feasible for linear models.
CONTROLS: Analyze the effect of the sampling distribution on the bounds, and compare the results on a linear model benchmark to those obtained with other estimators, such as LeverageSHAP.
COST: 2500
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the bounds will provide insightful comparisons between KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP on linear models, potentially revealing situations in which one estimator outperforms the other.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sampling without Replacement for KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: Develop and analyze a variant of KernelSHAP that samples subset rows without replacement from the original regression problem, in contrast to the original KernelSHAP estimator that samples with replacement.
CONTROLS: Compare the sampling without replacement variant against the original KernelSHAP estimator on a variety of real-world datasets, examining differences in bias, variance, and runtime.
COST: 3500
PREDICTION: We expect the sampling without replacement variant to potentially offer improved scalability and accuracy for KernelSHAP, but caution that reduced bias may also be accompanied by increased variance, leading to complex trade-offs.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Sampling without Replacement for KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: Develop a theoretical analysis of the sampling without replacement variant of KernelSHAP, examining how the absence of replacement affects the convergence rate of the estimator.
CONTROLS: Derive an expression for the variance of the sampling without replacement estimator and compare it to the variance of the original KernelSHAP estimator.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the sampling without replacement variant will exhibit faster convergence rates for large samples, but may experience slower convergence rates for small samples due to increased variance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Leverage Score Sampling for KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: Adapt the sampling method used in LeverageSHAP to KernelSHAP, and analyze the resulting estimator. This will involve defining a measure of leverage for each subset in the KernelSHAP regression problem and using these to inform the sampling process.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the leverage score sampling variant with the original KernelSHAP estimator on a range of real-world datasets.
COST: 4500
PREDICTION: We expect the leverage score sampling variant to potentially outperform the original KernelSHAP estimator, offering improved accuracy while requiring careful tuning of the leverage threshold.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Model-X KernelSHAP: Accounting for Model Uncertainty
PROPOSAL: Introduce model uncertainty into the KernelSHAP framework by treating the model as a random variable and deriving a Bayesian treatment of the KernelSHAP estimator.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of Model-X KernelSHAP with the original KernelSHAP estimator on a set of real-world benchmarks where multiple models are competing.
COST: 5500
PREDICTION: We anticipate that Model-X KernelSHAP will offer a valuable tool for accounting for model uncertainty in the context of feature attribution, but warn that the additional complexity may lead to computational challenges.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Leverage Score Sampling for KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: Provide a theoretical analysis of the leverage score sampling variant of KernelSHAP, examining how the sampling process affects the convergence rate and variance of the estimator.
CONTROLS: Derive an expression for the variance of the leverage score sampling estimator and compare it to the variance of the original KernelSHAP estimator.
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the leverage score sampling variant will offer improved convergence rates and reduced variance compared to the original KernelSHAP estimator, but the benefits may be contingent on the specific choice of leverage score threshold.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Temporal Attention in Multimodal Transformers for Temporal Change Description
PROPOSAL: We experiment with different attention mechanisms for temporally ordering the sequence of satellite images when using a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) for temporal change description. Specifically, we compare (1) a standard self-attention mechanism, (2) a hierarchical temporal attention mechanism that captures both short-term and long-term temporal relationships, and (3) an Inter-Predictor Attention mechanism inspired by ubiquitous learning, where the attention adaptively focuses on the image-pair interactions that the model is uncertain about.
CONTROLS: We evaluate our models on the standard language metrics (Bleu, ROUGE, METEOR) using the COSTAL Waste Scar dataset and the dynamic change description annotations provided by VaiDIA dataset.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: The hierarchical temporal attention will improve performance, potentially outperforming the standard self-attention (1-5 BLEU increase), and the Inter-Predictor Attention will produce more informative and accurate descriptions by effectively reducing the noise in the historical sequence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Combining Transformer-Based Image Modality Augmentation with Textual Guidance for Satellite Image Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We explore an approach that combines Transformer-based image modality augmentation with textual guidance to aid in the forecasting of future satellite images from a given time series. Specifically, we use a CLS Token-based image-text matching and then augment the images using a pre-trained image CLIP (Auto-encoder) to prevent overfitting. This method fuses low-level image features and contextual information from the text to enhance forecasting performance.
CONTROLS: As controls, we test the approach against a suite of state-of-the-art methods including conditional GAN-based, Mask R-CNN-based and avd degradation-based methods for a future time point forecasting task. We also perform an ablation study on the importance of removing the augmentation method and keeping the textual guidance constant.
COST: 750
PREDICTION: The proposed method should outperform state-of-the-art image forecasting models due to the added benefit of textual information, with a potential Relative Top-1 Metric improvement of 8.2% (expected failure in diminshing R1 metric by 0.55, observed in long-time #greyscale oscillations cases)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Understanding Long-Range Temporal Dynamics through Graph Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: We propose to represent the historical sequence of satellite images as a graph, where nodes correspond to individual images and edges model the relationships between consecutive images. We then use Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to capture the long-range temporal dependencies and evolve the graph incrementally to forecast the next image. This approach is specifically designed to handle sparse and irregularly sampled data.
CONTROLS: We compare GNNs-based forecasting against state-of-the-art stochastic processes-based approach for modeling temporal dependency.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: The GNNs-based forecasting approach will significantly improve forecasting quality on long-range dependencies and provide a better qualitative fit to satellite image sequences with vast intervals of missing dates, measured by 12.4 Mean Absolute Percentage Error drop.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Causal Temporal Reasoning for Satellite Image Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We develop a method that incorporates causal reasoning into the forecasting process, allowing the model to learn the underlying causal mechanisms driving changes in the satellite images. We use a combination of temporal graph logic and MCMC-based sampling to identify causal relationships between variables and use them to inform the forecasting process.
CONTROLS: We compare our method against a baseline that uses traditional temporal reasoning without considering causal relationships.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: The causal temporal reasoning method will improve forecasting accuracy, especially in scenarios with significant changes in the underlying context or environment, with a 9.5% relative improvement on test-set metrics and observed to provide up to 85% agreement between the predicted probabilities of explanation shocks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Temporal Consistency in Satellite Image Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel evaluation metric, Temporal Consistency Error (TCE), to measure the degree to which the forecasted image is consistent with the observed historical trends and dynamics. We also develop a set of qualitative evaluation tasks to assess visual coherence, temporal integrity, and change plausibility. Our evaluation framework is designed to complement existing image-quality metrics.
CONTROLS: We compare different forecasting models, including ours, using a combination of quantitative (TCE) and qualitative evaluation metrics.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: The proposed evaluation framework will reveal significant variation in temporal consistency across different forecasting models, with our method outperforming state-of-the-art models in terms of TCE and qualitative evaluation metrics by up to 25.6% in the signs used for breakthrough rain/growth tracking preferred manifestations.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Understanding Long-Range Temporal Dynamics through Graph Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal to incorporate the Temporal Consistency Error (TCE) metric as an additional loss term in the optimization process of the Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for forecasting. This allows the model to learn not only the long-range temporal dependencies but also to produce forecasts that are consistent with the observed historical trends and dynamics.
CONTROLS: We compare the revised GNNs-based forecasting approach against the original one without the TCE loss term.
COST: 1800 (updated from 1200)
PREDICTION: The revised GNNs-based forecasting approach will improve both forecasting quality and temporal consistency, measured by a 15.1% reduction in Mean Absolute Percentage Error and a 30.5% decrease in TCE, while minimizing divergent losses by 7.6 underestimated wildfires.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Incorporating Land-Cover Change Knowledge Graph into Satellite Image Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose to leverage a land-cover change knowledge graph to provide additional semantic information about the observed land changes and to guide the forecasting process. The knowledge graph is constructed based on a priori knowledge about land-cover changes and is used to condition the forecasting model to produce more informed and accurate forecasts.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach against a baseline that uses a forecasting model without access to the knowledge graph.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: The incorporation of the land-cover change knowledge graph will lead to significant improvements in forecasting accuracy, especially for rare or uncertain land-cover changes, with a 12.6% increase in relative top-1 metric compared to the baseline model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Weakly-Supervised Land-Cover Change Discovery using Pretrained MLLMs
PROPOSAL: We propose to use pre-trained Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to weakly supervise land-cover change discovery from satellite images. The MLLMs are fine-tuned on a small labeled dataset and then used to identify areas of interest where land-cover changes may have occurred. This approach reduces the need for extensive manual labeling and allows for large-scale exploration of land-cover changes.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach against a strong baseline that uses a fully-supervised land-cover change detection method.
COST: 700
PREDICTION: The weakly-supervised approach will discover land-cover changes at least as accurately as the fully-supervised baseline, while providing significant cost and scalability benefits, observed by 92.6% better normal mapping in fewer steps of learning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning from Multimodal Large Language Models for Satellite Image Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose to leverage pre-trained Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and adapt them for satellite image time series forecasting tasks. By using transfer learning, we aim to leverage the knowledge and representations learned by the MLLMs on large-scale multimodal datasets to improve forecasting performance.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach against a baseline that trains a model from scratch using only satellite image data.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: The transfer learning approach will lead to significant improvements in forecasting performance, especially for small.dataset sizes, measured by 24.4% increase in relative top-1 metric compared to the baseline model. Observed anomalies as initial boost of metric by 0.6 before getting diminished to normal effect.

TITLE: Ensemble Methods for Combining Individual Expertise in Satellite Image Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop an ensemble method that combines the strengths of individual models, including temporal attention, graph neural networks, causal reasoning, and transfer learning from multimodal language models. The ensemble approach aims to leverage the unique strengths of each model to improve forecasting performance.
CONTROLS: We compare our ensemble method against the individual models and a baseline that combines them without an ensemble framework.
COST: 2500
PREDICTION: The ensemble approach will lead to significant improvements in forecasting performance, measured by a 32.1% increase in relative top-1 metric compared to the baseline model, and will demonstrate a more robust and generalizable performance across various scenario evaluations for remaining jumps to unforseen terrain.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Reevaluating update components in OGD for time series forecasting
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether the standard update components, i.e., final-layer weights or adapters attached to a model's input or output, are indeed the best quantities to adapt in pre-trained forecasters. Compare updating these components versus updating model weights at different depth levels or adapting the ensemble weights of a model ensemble on real-world benchmarks in traffic flow forecasting and electricity consumption forecasting. Update the model parameters using a short-term (e.g., recent samples) and a long-term (e.g., samples aggregated over several time steps) adaptation strategy.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: OGD with standard update components; Baseline 2: Updating final-layer weights only; Baseline 3: Model-free updating, where the adapter module's weights are updated using only past predictions without reusing any learned model parameters; Ablation study 1: Remove short-term adaptation; Ablation study 2: Remove long-term adaptation.
COST: 15000
PREDICTION: Updating model weights at deeper levels or the ensemble weights may exhibit better adaptation performance, especially when the climate changes affect the traffic patterns, due to their ability to capture higher-level patterns in data. The model-free algorithm could be competitive in scenarios with strong patterns in data.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Adaptive weighting for ensemble models in online time series forecasting
PROPOSAL: Introduce an adaptive weighting scheme for ensemble models, allowing the weights of individual models to change as new data arrives. Evaluate the proposed adaptive weighting scheme on real-world benchmarks in various domains, including weather forecasting and solar power forecasting. The adaptive weighting scheme will update the weights based on the performance of each model on recent data using a online optimization method. The performance metrics will include forecast accuracy metrics (e.g., MAE, RMSE) and strength of the adaptation.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Static ensemble selection method; Baseline 2: Randomly chosen new weights; Ablation study 1: Weights updated only using recent data, ignoring performance on older data; Ablation study 2: Weights updated using a fixed schedule, not adapting to current task difficulty.
COST: 20000
PREDICTION: The adaptive weighting scheme should improve the performance over static ensemble selection method by adapting to changing task difficulty, though its effectiveness may vary depending on the task characteristics and quality of individual models in the ensemble.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Exploring novelty detection for concept drift mitigation
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novelty detection method for identifying instances of concept drift. Use an autoencoder-based anomaly detector to detect changes in the data distribution. Train the autoencoder on historical data and then use it to monitor incoming data in real-time. Act on the identified concept drift by updating the model or switching to a different model. Apply the novelty detection method on real-world benchmarks in traffic flow forecasting and electricity consumption forecasting to compare its effectiveness to existing methods for concept drift.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: OGD with periodic model retraining; Baseline 2: Ensembles with detection of ensemble members performance degradation; Ablation study 1: Remove online adaptation after novelty detection; Ablation study 2: Increase the threshold for novelty detection.
COST: 22000
PREDICTION: The novelty detection method can effectively identify instances of concept drift, which would allow the model to adapt to the changing patterns in data, reducing the harm caused by the drift. However, it would add complexity and delay, which could affect real-time predictions if not properly managed.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Exploring novelty detection for concept drift mitigation
PROPOSAL: Revise the novelty detection method to incorporate transfer learning and pre-trained models. When a concept drift is detected, fine-tune a pre-trained model on the new data instead of adapting the original model. This way, the benefits of pre-training can still be leveraged when adapting to changing patterns. Implement this revised novelty detection method on real-world benchmarks in weather forecasting and solar power forecasting to compare its effectiveness to existing methods and the original novelty detection method.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: OGD with periodic model retraining; Baseline 2: Ensembles with detection of ensemble members performance degradation; Ablation study 1: Compare adaptation speed with traditional adaptations; Ablation study 2: Validate against not fine-tuning, pre-training, occuring in interactive scenarios.
COST: 25000
PREDICTION: The revised novelty detection with fine-tuning can lead to a faster adaptation and coping with changing environments, providing benefits particularly in areas with concept drifts due to patterns resulting by sudden and transient information.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Investigating self-supervised online learning for transfer learning
PROPOSAL: Introduce a self-supervised online learning paradigm for transfer learning, where the model is trained on auxiliary tasks during deployment to adapt to changing patterns. The auxiliary tasks can be constructed by creating tasks such as incomplete data estimation, ask data similarity and relation or even property asking a relation unknown for model training at the invention stage. Evaluate the effectiveness of this approach on real-world benchmarks in exchange rate forecasting and electricity transformer temperature forecasting, comparing it to traditional transfer learning and pre-training methods.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Traditional transfer learning with pre-trained models; Baseline 2: Self-supervised pre-training on auxiliary tasks before deployment; Ablation study 1: Remove self-supervised online learning; Ablation study 2: Reduce the number and complexity of auxiliary tasks.
COST: 28000
PREDICTION: The self-supervised online learning paradigm can enable adaptation to changing patterns and improve transfer learning, especially when dealing with transient and sudden information releases in real-world forecasting scenarios, potentially by recovering relatively full and consistent diverse training sets.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Investigating self-supervised online learning for transfer learning
PROPOSAL: Revise the self-supervised online learning paradigm to include a meta-learning stage, where the model is trained to learn how to adapt to different tasks and patterns. During the meta-learning stage, the model is trained on a set of different auxiliary tasks and environments, and then fine-tuned on the actual task at hand. This allows the model to learn a more general adaptation strategy that can be applied to a wide range of tasks and environments. Implement this revised paradigm on real-world benchmarks in traffic flow forecasting and weather forecasting.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Traditional transfer learning with pre-trained models; Baseline 2: Self-supervised pre-training on auxiliary tasks before deployment; Ablation study 1: Remove meta-learning stage; Ablation study 2: Reduce the number and diversity of auxiliary tasks.
COST: 32000
PREDICTION: The revised self-supervised online learning paradigm with meta-learning can enable more effective and flexible adaptation to changing patterns and environments, potentially leading to state-of-the-art performance in real-world forecasting scenarios with concept drift and novelty.

TITLE: Multitask learning for online time series forecasting
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of multitask learning for online time series forecasting, where a single model is trained to perform multiple tasks simultaneously, such as forecasting multiple related time series or forecasting multiple steps ahead. This can allow the model to share knowledge and transferred learning across tasks and time steps. Evaluate the effectiveness of multitask learning on real-world benchmarks in electricity consumption forecasting and solar power forecasting, comparing it to traditional single-task learning approaches.

PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of online transfer learning for domain adaptation in time series forecasting, where a model trained on one domain (e.g., country, region) is adapted to perform well on a different domain (e.g., country, region) with a different data distribution. This can involve finetuning the model on the new domain, or using a domain adaptation layer to learn a new representation of the data. However, it may require significant expertise to design and train the domain adaptation layer.

TITLE: Quantization Overhead Analysis of LoRA Fine-tuning
PROPOSAL: We employ a combination of theoretical analysis and experimental study to investigate the quantization overhead of FP8 arithmetic applied to LoRA fine-tuning. For the theoretical part, we derive a formula to estimate the quantization overhead as a function of matrix size, rank, and the specific FP8 format used. For the experimental part, we select a range of popular LLM models and corresponding datasets for LoRA fine-tuning, specifically instruction tuning for LLM chat assistants, multitask knowledge question answering, and commonsense reasoning question answering. We compare the quantization overhead of different FP8 formats (E4M3 and E5M2) against the baseline of standard FP32 arithmetic, measuring the additional costs in terms of both time and memory. To control for the variability of adapter ranks and matrix sizes, we perform ablation studies by fixing the rank and randomly perturbing the matrix size, and vice versa.

COST: 2400
PREDICTION: We expect the quantization overhead to be substantial (10-30%) for small adapter ranks and matrix sizes, but decrease rapidly as the rank and matrix size increase beyond 64x64. The error bounds should exhibit significant variability across different FP8 formats, due to the vastly different representable ranges and maximum absolute values of their exponent and mantissa components.
